claims.claim: A Laravel endpoint that queries MySQL usually manages a few hundred requests per second per core
claims.measured: php-laravel: 149 req/s for one Postgres row and 93 req/s for 20 queries on 1 CPU (681 req/s plaintext)
claims.why: The measured 149 req/s per core with one query is a bit under 'a few hundred' but within a factor of 2, and the uncached Laravel figure on 2 cores (about 300 req/s) is far below 3,000.

claims.claim: The uncached numbers don't fit on this box either way: a rewrite in Go or Node would still be bound by database round trips and wouldn't reach about 1,500 requests/second per core
claims.about: Go (go-gin, go-nethttp) and Node (node-express, node-fastify) compared with Laravel
claims.measured: One DB row per request: go-gin 22,138, go-nethttp 19,543, node-fastify 9,423, node-express 9,034 req/s per core; 20 queries: go-nethttp 2,631, node-express 1,062 req/s per core
claims.why: Go and Node each handled 6 to 15 times the 1,500 req/s per core needed on the single-query endpoint, so 3,000 req/s uncached fits easily on 2 vCPUs, and changing language would close the gap.

claims.claim: Octane or FrankenPHP keep PHP workers alive and can multiply throughput
claims.measured: Octane vs FPM: one DB row 732 vs 149 (4.9x); plaintext 1,172 vs 681 (1.7x); JSON 1,224 vs 705 (1.7x); 20 queries 123 vs 93 (1.3x); but 10 ms I/O wait 86 vs 591 (worse)
claims.why: Octane gave 1.3x to 4.9x higher throughput in most tests, including about 5x on the single-query endpoint, but it was much worse in the I/O-wait test, and FrankenPHP was not measured.

claims.claim: Each PHP-FPM child can use tens of megabytes
claims.why: The measurements give memory for the whole container (52 MB idle, 58–75 MB peak) but not the number of workers or memory per worker.
